title: Suitability and quality of the measures to maximise expected outcomes and impacts, as set out in the dissemination and exploitation plan, including communication activities
content:
## 2.2 Suitability and quality of the measures to maximise expected outcomes and impacts, as set out in the dissemination and exploitation plan, including communication activities

**Overall logic and proportionality.** FIELDWISE is a single-researcher European Postdoctoral Fellowship hosted by Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), with a six-month non-academic placement at AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság closing the action. Its measures to maximise outcomes and impact are therefore scaled to one fellow and one host, not to a large consortium, and are organised as three distinct but connected streams: **dissemination** of validated results to audiences that can build on or use them; **exploitation** of the project's assets along an explicit research-to-operation path; and **communication** of the work to growers, advisors and the wider public. Each stream names its target group, is anchored to a specific project deliverable or KPI wherever the call permits, and is resourced from a continuous cross-cutting effort strand covering management, training and dissemination across the whole 30-month action, so the plan is a costed commitment rather than an aspiration. This design directly answers the criticism recorded against the researcher's previous submission that the economic and technological route to users and the IP strategy were insufficiently substantiated.

**Dissemination to scientific and professional users, with target groups.** The primary dissemination channel is peer-reviewed open-access publication. The publications programme is planned around four principal outputs (P1–P4), with at least two peer-reviewed submissions during or shortly after the fellowship, all made openly accessible in line with Horizon Europe and MSCA open-science requirements. The target audiences are precise: the agricultural remote-sensing and plant-physiology research community (Earth-observation-for-agriculture scientists and hyperspectral proximal-sensing researchers) for the methodological results on transferable hyperspectral-to-Sentinel-2 features and temporal water-stress forecasting. Beyond narrative publication, FIELDWISE disseminates reusable research assets: the Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library (D2.2), released with an explicit transferable-or-hyperspectral-only verdict for every candidate feature (tracked by KPI K2); the FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card (D3.2), released with a published model card documenting the engine (KPI K4); and the Adaptation protocol (D4.3), which states the minimum local-calibration volume needed to move the approach to a new agro-environment (KPI K6). These assets are aimed at European research organisations and precision-agriculture model developers seeking reusable transfer features and forecasting engines, and they are the concrete mechanism by which FIELDWISE contributes to increased R&I capacity, output and knowledge transfer among European research organisations (expected impact EI-05). The cross-country evidence — the Hungary→Bulgaria transferability report (D4.2) and the Adaptation protocol (D4.3) — is shared directly with the international partner, the Институт по зеленчукови култури „Марица“ – Пловдив, and specifically reported to Prof. Vinelina Yankova (KPI K5), extending the results to the wider Bulgarian and Hungarian processing-tomato research and advisory community. Underpinning all of this, the harmonised multi-season archive (D1.1) is curated to be FAIR — findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable — with documented QC flags and metadata, and data management follows a data-management plan maintained to MSCA open-science practice; any data or feature exchange with the transferability and validation partners respects the partners' agreed access conditions.

**Communication to the public and to the farming community.** Communication activities address audiences beyond scientific peers and are proportionate to a single-fellow action. FIELDWISE will run one public field demonstration of the web MVP with growers working with AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság, and will produce one public-facing article per project year, targeting processing-tomato growers, farm advisors and the interested general agricultural public. This is the project's route to broadened public engagement with research (expected impact EI-03) and to the enhanced networking and communication capacity with the general public that the call sets as a postdoctoral outcome. Communication is reinforced through education: the fellow will co-design and deliver a full module unit within an ELTE MSc course on Earth observation for agriculture, and will co-supervise the field-experiment component of one PhD student's work, feeding validated results into higher-education teaching (expected impact EI-06) and reaching ELTE MSc students and teaching staff.

**Exploitation and the research-to-operation path.** Exploitation is structured as a staged path from a desktop research prototype to an externally evaluated operational demonstrator, and it is what makes the impact claims credible rather than speculative. The scientifically validated predictions are translated into the DrR web MVP (D5.1), serving stress probability, uncertainty, spatial risk, irrigation priority and temporal evolution (KPI K7). The MVP is then subjected to independent, inter-sectoral scrutiny: the AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation (D5.4) assesses it across all nine assessment dimensions and provides external evidence about whether the technology meets actual agricultural software requirements (KPI K9). Finally, the FMIS integration roadmap (D5.5) names the required interfaces and the concrete post-fellowship steps needed to embed FIELDWISE outputs into farm management information systems (KPI K10). The six-month placement is the exploitation engine here: written from inside the implementing company, it grounds the roadmap and the operational assessment in a production FMIS environment and in requirements engineering and user testing with commercial growers, so the exploitation route is informed by a real commercial software practice rather than by assumption. The proposal is explicit about the boundary of what the fellowship promises — the MVP is the research-to-operation demonstrator, not the primary scientific objective, and full commercial integration is not promised within the action — which keeps the exploitation claim honest.

**Intellectual-property management and protection measures.** The project has no separately negotiated IP register at proposal stage; the IP position is therefore stated as a clear default appropriate to an MSCA postdoctoral fellowship and refined through the action. Ownership of results defaults to the host, ELTE, with the fellow as author-inventor, and open dissemination of scientific results — open-access publications, the released transfer library, and the published model card — is the primary route to impact. Where the web MVP or predictive engine shows commercialisation potential, protection would rely first on copyright in the software and on trade secrets around calibration data, with patenting considered only if the AgroVIR evaluation identifies protectable, novel technical subject matter; this proportionate, dissemination-first posture avoids over-claiming protection the project cannot yet substantiate. Access to and use of the transferability-partner and validation-partner data are governed by the partners' agreed conditions: farmer yields, irrigation records and field geometries are commercially sensitive and are handled under a data-sharing agreement, with results published only in aggregated or anonymised form. One background-IP point is deliberately surfaced rather than concealed: the DrR – Digital Agronomist components originate as the fellow's own pre-existing prototype and are treated as her background IP, so the ownership of work performed on those components during the placement inside a commercial partner must be fixed in the placement and partnership agreements before the placement begins; this remains to be settled at agreement stage and is flagged here as an open IP-management item rather than presented as resolved.

**Concrete actions during and after the project; sustainability.** During the action, each dissemination and exploitation activity is bound to a named deliverable and, where the instrument allows, to a measurable KPI, so progress is auditable at the five steering points. After the action, results persist through several concrete mechanisms: the released predictive engine and model card (D3.2) and the harmonised archive (D1.1) remain maintained, FAIR outputs held at ELTE; the transfer library (D2.2) and Adaptation protocol (D4.3), with their stated local-calibration cost, provide a documented method for transferring the approach to further crops and regions; the FMIS integration roadmap (D5.5), grounded in the external AgroVIR evaluation, defines the post-fellowship steps toward operational use; and the co-designed ELTE MSc module unit embeds the project's methods into ongoing teaching. ELTE, Magyar Agrár- és Élettudományi Egyetem, the Институт по зеленчукови култури „Марица“ – Пловдив and AGROVIR Üzletviteli Tanácsadó Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság each carry a share of this sustainability. Taken together, the measures are matched to the scale of a single-researcher fellowship, address clearly identified target groups, and turn the project's outputs into durable scientific, operational and public value.

These communication measures address the call's postdoctoral outcome of enhanced networking and communication capacity with the general public.

The six-month placement grounds D5.4 and D5.5 in a production FMIS environment with requirements engineering and user testing with commercial growers.

Each dissemination/exploitation activity is bound to a named deliverable and, where permitted, a KPI (K2, K4, K6, K7, K9, K10), making progress auditable.
